blocks.text: A person who is running from danger, a child lying in deep sleep while growing, and a patient on months of high-dose steroid tablets all show the same principle: hormones decide whether the body is spending its fuel on building or on survival. Growth hormone builds, adrenaline mobilises within seconds, and cortisol sustains the response for hours and, in excess, slowly dismantles the body.

blocks.markdown:
**Growth hormone (GH).** GH is a protein hormone from **somatotrophs** of the anterior pituitary. It is released in **pulses**, with the largest pulse during deep (slow-wave) sleep. Control comes from two hypothalamic peptides: **GHRH** stimulates GH and **somatostatin** inhibits it; **ghrelin** (from the stomach) also stimulates release.

- **Stimulated by:** deep sleep, exercise, hypoglycaemia, fasting, some amino acids (arginine), sex steroids and stress.
- **Inhibited by:** hyperglycaemia, obesity and raised **IGF-1** (negative feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary).

GH has two kinds of action. **Indirect (growth-promoting):** GH stimulates the liver, and local tissues, to make **insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)**, which promotes growth of cartilage and bone at the epiphyseal plates and protein synthesis in muscle. **Direct (metabolic):** GH raises plasma glucose and free fatty acids: it promotes **lipolysis** and reduces glucose uptake by muscle and fat (an insulin-antagonist, 'diabetogenic' effect), and it increases hepatic glucose output.

blocks.title: Gigantism and acromegaly
blocks.text: Excess GH, most often from a pituitary adenoma, causes gigantism when it begins in childhood before the epiphyseal growth plates fuse (excessive linear growth) and acromegaly when it begins in adults (enlargement of hands, feet and jaw, coarse facial features and soft tissue overgrowth). Deficiency in childhood causes short stature with proportionate growth failure.

blocks.markdown:
**The stress response.** Stress activates two arms that act on different time scales.

**The sympatho-adrenal medullary arm (seconds).** Preganglionic sympathetic fibres release acetylcholine onto **chromaffin cells** of the **adrenal medulla**, which secrete **adrenaline** (about 80%) and noradrenaline into blood. Adrenaline acts on adrenergic receptors:

- **Beta-1:** increased heart rate and contractility, raising cardiac output.
- **Beta-2:** bronchodilation and vasodilation in skeletal muscle and liver.
- **Alpha-1:** vasoconstriction in skin and gut, diverting blood to muscle.
- **Metabolic:** glycogenolysis in liver and muscle, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, increased glucagon and decreased insulin secretion, so plasma glucose and fatty acids rise.

**The HPA arm (minutes to hours).** CRH drives ACTH and **cortisol** from the adrenal cortex (the axis itself is covered in the adrenal and thyroid axes unit). Cortisol is essential for survival during sustained stress.

**Actions of cortisol.** Cortisol acts through intracellular receptors to change gene expression, so its effects take hours. It is catabolic in most tissues, with the aim of keeping glucose available for the brain.

- **Glucose:** increases hepatic **gluconeogenesis** and reduces glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat, raising plasma glucose.
- **Protein:** promotes breakdown of muscle protein to supply amino acids for gluconeogenesis; thins skin and connective tissue; inhibits bone formation.
- **Fat:** promotes lipolysis but redistributes fat to the trunk, face and upper back.
- **Cardiovascular:** **permissive** for the vascular response to catecholamines and maintains blood pressure and sodium retention (at high levels it also acts at the mineralocorticoid receptor).
- **Immune:** suppresses inflammation and the immune response; this is the basis of glucocorticoid drug therapy.
- **Other:** promotes fetal lung maturation and affects mood and cognition.

blocks.caption: Metabolic and cardiovascular effects of the main stress and growth hormones.
rows: Heart rate and contractility up; bronchodilation; skin and gut vasoconstriction

blocks.caption: Cardiac output (CO, L/min) equals heart rate (HR, beats/min) multiplied by stroke volume (SV, L/beat).

blocks.title: Cardiac output during an adrenaline surge
blocks.prompt: At rest a person has a heart rate of 65 beats/min and a stroke volume of 75 mL. During an adrenaline surge heart rate rises to 120 beats/min and stroke volume to 90 mL. Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the surge.

steps.text: Convert stroke volume to litres: 75 mL = 0.075 L and 90 mL = 0.090 L.
Interpret: adrenaline acting on beta-1 receptors more than doubles cardiac output, delivering more blood to the muscles.

blocks.answer: About 4.9 L/min at rest and 10.8 L/min during the surge, an increase of about 5.9 L/min.

blocks.markdown:
**Cushing syndrome.** Cushing syndrome is the clinical state caused by prolonged exposure to excess glucocorticoid. The commonest cause is **glucocorticoid medication**. Endogenous causes are an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease), ectopic ACTH from a tumour elsewhere, or a cortisol-secreting adrenal tumour. Each feature follows from an action of cortisol:

- Central obesity, round (moon) face and fat pad on the upper back: **lipolysis with redistribution**.
- Thin skin, easy bruising and purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, osteoporosis: **protein catabolism and loss of connective tissue and bone matrix**.
- Hyperglycaemia (diabetes): **gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance**.
- Hypertension: **sodium retention, mineralocorticoid action and amplified vascular catecholamine response**.
- Infections and poor wound healing: **immunosuppression**.
- Mood disturbance: **central effects**.

blocks.title: Steroid potency conversion (pharmacology teaching example)
blocks.prompt: Equivalent anti-inflammatory doses are about hydrocortisone 20 mg = prednisolone 5 mg. A patient takes prednisolone 10 mg daily. Express this as a hydrocortisone equivalent, and compare with the normal adult cortisol production of about 15-25 mg/day of hydrocortisone equivalent.

steps.text: Find the conversion factor: 20 mg hydrocortisone corresponds to 5 mg prednisolone, a factor of 4.
Compare: 40 mg is roughly twice the physiological daily production, so prolonged therapy would produce Cushingoid features and suppress the patient's own ACTH and adrenal function.

blocks.answer: 10 mg prednisolone is equivalent to about 40 mg hydrocortisone per day, roughly twice physiological output.

items: GH release is pulsatile, highest in deep sleep; GHRH stimulates, somatostatin and IGF-1 inhibit.
IGF-1 mediates growth; GH itself is lipolytic and raises glucose (insulin antagonism).
Adrenaline: seconds, beta-1 cardiac effects, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, redistributes blood flow.
Cortisol: hours, gluconeogenesis, protein catabolism, permissive and anti-inflammatory.
Cushing syndrome: excess cortisol, most often from steroid drugs.

blocks.title: Adrenaline versus cortisol
blocks.text: Adrenaline gives the fast response through receptors on the cell membrane in seconds, while cortisol gives the sustained response through intracellular receptors and gene expression over hours. Cortisol also makes the vessels and heart responsive to catecholamines (a permissive action), so without cortisol stress can cause circulatory collapse.

blocks.title: Do not confuse GH with IGF-1
blocks.text: The growth-promoting effect on bone is largely mediated by IGF-1 made in response to GH. GH itself acts against insulin and raises glucose, which is why acromegaly often causes diabetes and why GH is suppressed after a glucose load in healthy people.

points: GH is released in pulses (peak in deep sleep) under GHRH and somatostatin control, and acts both directly (lipolysis, glucose-raising) and through IGF-1 (growth).
Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla produces fast cardiovascular and metabolic effects via beta and alpha receptors, including increased cardiac output and glycogenolysis.
Cortisol produces slower catabolic effects: gluconeogenesis, insulin resistance, protein breakdown, fat redistribution, and is permissive and anti-inflammatory.
Cushing syndrome results from chronic excess cortisol (most commonly from steroid drugs) and every feature maps to a normal action of cortisol.

questions.stem: Which substance, produced mainly by the liver under the influence of growth hormone, mediates most of the growth-promoting effects of GH on bone?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: IGF-1 mediates the growth-promoting actions of GH.
distractorRationale.c: Ghrelin stimulates GH release but does not mediate growth effects.
distractorRationale.d: Calcitonin is a calcium-lowering hormone from the thyroid C cells.

questions.explanation: GH stimulates the liver, and other tissues, to secrete IGF-1, which promotes growth of cartilage and bone at the epiphyseal plates and increases protein synthesis. IGF-1 also exerts negative feedback on GH secretion.

questions.stem: Which stimulus decreases growth hormone secretion?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hyperglycaemia suppresses GH, which is the basis of a glucose suppression test.
distractorRationale.b: Deep sleep produces the largest GH pulse.

questions.explanation: GH is raised by fasting, hypoglycaemia, exercise and deep sleep and suppressed by hyperglycaemia and by IGF-1. This makes sense because GH is itself a glucose-raising hormone.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is 2.1 m tall with a rapidly increasing height and is found to have a pituitary adenoma secreting excess GH. Why does this condition cause gigantism rather than acromegaly?

options.text: The epiphyseal growth plates are still open, so excess GH and IGF-1 produce excessive linear growth
The tumour secretes IGF-1 rather than GH
Children lack GH receptors in the liver
The excess is of cortisol rather than GH

questions.correctOptionText: The epiphyseal growth plates are still open, so excess GH and IGF-1 produce excessive linear growth

distractorRationale.a: Correct: before fusion, bones can lengthen.
distractorRationale.b: The tumour secretes GH; IGF-1 rises secondarily.
distractorRationale.c: Children have GH receptors in the liver and elsewhere.
distractorRationale.d: The stem states the tumour secretes GH.

questions.explanation: Linear growth is possible only while the epiphyseal plates remain open. In adults, whose plates have fused, excess GH causes acromegaly with enlargement of the hands, feet and jaw rather than increased height.

questions.stem: Which combination of effects is characteristic of an adrenaline surge during acute stress?

options.text: Increased heart rate, bronchodilation, hepatic glycogenolysis and skin vasoconstriction
Decreased heart rate, bronchoconstriction and increased insulin secretion
Increased protein synthesis in muscle and lowering of blood glucose

questions.correctOptionText: Increased heart rate, bronchodilation, hepatic glycogenolysis and skin vasoconstriction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beta-1, beta-2 and alpha-1 actions together prepare for fight or flight.
distractorRationale.b: Adrenaline raises heart rate, dilates airways and reduces insulin secretion.
distractorRationale.c: Adrenaline increases glycogenolysis and constricts gut vessels.
distractorRationale.d: Adrenaline mobilises fuel and raises glucose; it is catabolic.

questions.explanation: Adrenaline acts on beta-1 receptors (heart rate, contractility), beta-2 receptors (bronchodilation, muscle vasodilation), alpha-1 receptors (skin and gut vasoconstriction) and promotes glycogenolysis and lipolysis, raising glucose and fatty acids.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has weight gain around the trunk, purple abdominal stretch marks, easy bruising, difficulty rising from a chair, blood pressure 160/100 mmHg and raised fasting glucose. Which cortisol action best explains the difficulty rising from a chair?

options.text: Catabolism of muscle protein causing proximal myopathy
Increased lipolysis in subcutaneous fat of the limbs
Excess adrenaline acting on beta-2 receptors

questions.correctOptionText: Catabolism of muscle protein causing proximal myopathy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: breakdown of muscle protein for gluconeogenesis weakens large proximal muscles.
distractorRationale.c: Cortisol reduces, not increases, insulin sensitivity.
distractorRationale.d: The picture is of cortisol excess, not adrenaline excess.

questions.explanation: The features indicate Cushing syndrome. Cortisol promotes protein breakdown in muscle to provide amino acids for gluconeogenesis, so proximal muscles such as the thighs weaken, producing difficulty rising from a chair.

questions.stem: Cortisol increases the sensitivity of muscle and fat to insulin, thereby lowering blood glucose.
questions.explanation: Cortisol reduces glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis, so it raises blood glucose. Chronic excess therefore predisposes to diabetes.

questions.stem: Equivalent anti-inflammatory doses are about 20 mg hydrocortisone and 5 mg prednisolone. What daily hydrocortisone-equivalent dose, in mg, corresponds to 15 mg of prednisolone per day (a pharmacology teaching example)?
questions.explanation: The conversion factor is 20/5 = 4, so 15 mg of prednisolone corresponds to 15 x 4 = 60 mg of hydrocortisone. This is about three times the normal daily cortisol production, so prolonged use risks Cushingoid features.

questions.stem: During an adrenaline surge, a person's heart rate is 110 beats/min and stroke volume is 80 mL. Calculate the cardiac output in L/min.
questions.explanation: Cardiac output equals heart rate times stroke volume: 110 beats/min x 0.080 L = 8.8 L/min. This is substantially higher than a typical resting output of about 5 L/min, consistent with beta-1 stimulation.

questions.stem: Describe how growth hormone secretion is regulated and explain its direct metabolic effects and its indirect growth-promoting effects through IGF-1.
markingGuide: GH is released from anterior pituitary somatotrophs in pulses, largest in deep sleep
GHRH stimulates and somatostatin inhibits release; ghrelin stimulates
Stimuli include hypoglycaemia, fasting, exercise and some amino acids; hyperglycaemia and IGF-1 inhibit
Indirect: GH stimulates IGF-1 production (liver and tissues), which promotes growth of bone and cartilage at the epiphyseal plates and protein synthesis
Direct: lipolysis, reduced glucose uptake in muscle and fat (insulin antagonism) and increased hepatic glucose output, raising plasma glucose
IGF-1 feeds back negatively on hypothalamus and pituitary
questions.explanation: GH links the nutritional state to growth. It raises glucose and free fatty acids directly while IGF-1 mediates the growth effects, which is why GH excess can cause both tall stature or acromegaly and diabetes.

questions.stem: Explain how each of the following features of Cushing syndrome arises from the physiological actions of cortisol: central obesity, easy bruising with purple striae, hyperglycaemia and hypertension. Name the commonest cause.
markingGuide: Commonest cause is glucocorticoid medication; endogenous causes include ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, ectopic ACTH, adrenal tumour
Central obesity: lipolysis with redistribution of fat to trunk, face and upper back
Bruising and striae: protein catabolism causes thinning of skin and loss of collagen and connective tissue
Hyperglycaemia: increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and reduced insulin sensitivity of muscle and fat
Hypertension: sodium and water retention via mineralocorticoid-receptor action at high cortisol levels and permissive amplification of catecholamine vasoconstriction
Other features follow from catabolism and immunosuppression: myopathy, osteoporosis, infections
questions.explanation: Cushing syndrome is the exaggeration of the normal catabolic, glucose-raising and permissive actions of cortisol. Linking each sign to its mechanism makes the syndrome predictable rather than a list to memorise.
